mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes sp hybridisation?

options.A: One s orbital mixes with one p orbital to give two sp hybrid orbitals arranged linearly (180°).
options.B: One s orbital mixes with two p orbitals to give three sp2 hybrid orbitals arranged trigonal planar (120°).
options.C: One s orbital mixes with three p orbitals to give four sp3 hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedral (109.5°).
options.D: One s orbital mixes with one p and one d orbital to give three dsp hybrid orbitals.

mcqs.answer: One s orbital mixes with one p orbital to give two sp hybrid orbitals arranged linearly (180°).
mcqs.explanation: In sp hybridisation, one s and one p orbital combine, producing two equivalent sp hybrids that lie opposite each other, giving a linear geometry with a bond angle of 180°. Options B and C describe sp2 and sp3 hybridisation respectively, while D is not relevant for main‑group elements in this context.

mcqs.question: In sp2 hybridisation, how many hybrid orbitals are formed and what is the resulting molecular geometry?

options.A: Three sp2 hybrid orbitals are formed; the geometry is trigonal planar with bond angles of about 120°.
options.B: Two sp2 hybrid orbitals are formed; the geometry is linear with bond angles of 180°.
options.C: Four sp2 hybrid orbitals are formed; the geometry is tetrahedral with bond angles of 109.5°.
options.D: One sp2 hybrid orbital is formed; the geometry is bent with bond angles of about 104.5°.

mcqs.answer: Three sp2 hybrid orbitals are formed; the geometry is trigonal planar with bond angles of about 120°.
mcqs.explanation: sp2 hybridisation involves mixing one s and two p orbitals, yielding three equivalent sp2 hybrids that lie in one plane, giving a trigonal planar arrangement (≈120°). The remaining unhybridised p orbital can form a π bond. The other options describe different hybridisations or geometries.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes sp3 hybridisation from sp2 hybridisation?

options.A: sp3 hybridisation produces four equivalent orbitals arranged tetrahedrally, whereas sp2 produces three orbitals in a trigonal planar arrangement.
options.B: sp3 hybridisation produces three equivalent orbitals arranged trigonal planar, whereas sp2 produces four orbitals in a tetrahedral arrangement.
options.C: Both sp3 and sp2 hybridisations give the same number of orbitals but differ only in bond angles.
options.D: sp3 hybridisation involves d‑orbitals, while sp2 hybridisation does not.

mcqs.answer: sp3 hybridisation produces four equivalent orbitals arranged tetrahedrally, whereas sp2 produces three orbitals in a trigonal planar arrangement.
mcqs.explanation: In sp3 hybridisation, one s and three p orbitals combine to give four equivalent sp3 hybrids directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5°). In sp2, one s and two p orbitals give three hybrids in a plane (120°). Options B, C, and D are incorrect descriptions.

mcqs.question: The molecule BF₃ exhibits bond angles of 120°. Which hybridisation of the central boron atom best explains this geometry?
mcqs.explanation: Boron in BF₃ forms three σ bonds with fluorine atoms. To accommodate three equivalent bonds with 120° angles, boron uses sp2 hybridisation, producing three planar sp2 hybrids. sp would give linear geometry, sp3 would give tetrahedral, and dsp2 is not applicable for boron.

mcqs.question: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in the molecule ethene (C₂H₄)?
mcqs.explanation: Each carbon in ethene forms three σ bonds (two C–H and one C–C) and one π bond. To make three σ bonds in a planar arrangement, each carbon undergoes sp2 hybridisation, giving three sp2 hybrids (120°) and leaving one unhybridised p orbital for the π bond. sp would give only two σ bonds, sp3 would give four σ bonds, and dsp2 is not relevant here.

mcqs.question: A molecule X has a central atom that forms exactly two sigma bonds and possesses no lone pairs. The observed bond angle is 180°. Which hybridisation is most likely for the central atom?
mcqs.explanation: When a central atom forms two sigma bonds with no lone pairs and the geometry is linear (180°), the atom uses sp hybridisation: one s and one p orbital combine to give two sp hybrids directed opposite each other. sp2 would give a trigonal planar arrangement, sp3 a tetrahedral one, and dsp3 involves d orbitals and is not needed for such simple bonding.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements reflects a common misconception about sp2 hybridisation?

options.A: sp2 hybridisation results in three equivalent hybrid orbitals arranged in a trigonal planar geometry.
options.B: One unhybridised p orbital remains after sp2 hybridisation and can participate in π bonding.
options.C: All three sp2 hybrid orbitals are used exclusively for σ bonds, leaving no orbital for π bonding.
options.D: The bond angles between the sp2 hybrid orbitals are approximately 120°.

mcqs.answer: All three sp2 hybrid orbitals are used exclusively for σ bonds, leaving no orbital for π bonding.
mcqs.explanation: The misconception is that sp2 hybridisation consumes all three orbitals for σ bonds, ignoring the remaining unhybridised p orbital that forms the π bond. Options A, B, and D correctly describe sp2 hybridisation, while C incorrectly states that no π bond can form.

mcqs.question: Why does methane (CH₄) adopt a tetrahedral shape?

options.A: Because carbon undergoes sp3 hybridisation, forming four equivalent orbitals directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
options.B: Because carbon uses sp2 hybridisation, producing three orbitals in a plane and one lone pair that pushes the fourth bond out of the plane.
options.C: Because the presence of lone pairs on carbon forces the bonds to adopt a tetrahedral arrangement.
options.D: Because d‑orbitals of carbon are involved, leading to a tetrahedral geometry.

mcqs.answer: Because carbon undergoes sp3 hybridisation, forming four equivalent orbitals directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
mcqs.explanation: In methane, carbon forms four σ bonds with hydrogen atoms. To accommodate four equivalent bonds with maximum separation, carbon hybridises its 2s and three 2p orbitals to produce four sp3 hybrids arranged tetrahedrally (109.5°). Options B and C incorrectly invoke sp2 or lone pairs (carbon has none), and D incorrectly suggests d‑orbital participation, which does not occur for second‑period elements.
